procedural_history.originating_court: Additional District and Sessions Judge, Nainital
procedural_history.impugned_order: The High Court's judgment dismissing the application for cancellation of bail, which included observations and directions that are now being challenged.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Appellant applied for bail before the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Nainital, which was rejected.
2. Appellant then pleaded his case for bail before the High Court.
3. The High Court allowed the bail application on June 8, 2021.
4. The complainant sought cancellation of the bail order by way of Bail Cancellation Application No.24/2022.
5. The High Court dismissed the application for cancellation of bail but made observations and issued directions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment dismissing the application for cancellation of bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The direction of the High Court of Uttarakhand in regard to registering a complaint against the present appellant is set aside.
Any proceedings arising therefrom shall stand quashed.
The decision in this appeal shall have no bearing on the criminal case pending against the appellant which shall proceed on its own merits as per law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the contents of the affidavit filed before the High Court constitutes an offence under Section 193 IPC, as defined in Section 191 IPC?

facts: The appellant was accused in an FIR and had been granted bail by the High Court.
In a subsequent bail cancellation application filed by the complainant, the High Court observed that the appellant had intentionally filed a false affidavit.
Based on this observation, the High Court directed its Registrar to file a complaint against the appellant for the offence of giving false evidence under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
law: The offence of giving false evidence is defined in Section 191 IPC and punished under Section 193 IPC.
To constitute an offence under Section 193 IPC, there must be a false statement made on oath in a judicial proceeding.
The Supreme Court clarified that mere suspicion or inaccurate statements are not sufficient to attract the offence; there must be a deliberate attempt or malafide intention to be proven.
application: The Court examined the statement made by the appellant in the affidavit and characterized it as a "denial simpliciter" of the allegations made by the complainant.
It found that this simple denial did not meet the threshold for perjury, particularly because there was no evidence of "malafide intention/deliberate attempt" on the part of the appellant.
The Court reasoned that the appellant's affidavit was merely his attempt to state his own version of events and deny the complainant's narrative.

Furthermore, the Court determined that initiating a prosecution for perjury in this situation was not "expedient in the interest of justice" and that the case did not present the exceptional circumstances required to invoke such a serious charge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's finding, concluding that the contents of the appellant's affidavit did not constitute an offence under Section 193 IPC. The Court held that the statement was a simple denial without malicious intent, and prosecuting it as perjury would be unjust. Consequently, the direction to file a complaint against the appellant was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the contents of the affidavit filed before the High Court constitutes an offence under Section 193 IPC, as defined in Section 191 IPC?
appellant_arguments: The statements made in the affidavit do not make it expedient in the interest of justice to initiate prosecution for filing a false affidavit.
The circumstances do not constitute the exceptional conditions required to invoke the powers to prosecute for filing a false affidavit, and therefore, such a prosecution would be unjust.
respondent_arguments: The appellant intentionally filed a false affidavit before the court, as evidenced by contradictory statements made therein.

statutes.section: A section defining false evidence, including Explanation 1 and Explanation 2.

cases.case_name: Dr. S.P. Kohli, Civil Surgeon, Ferozepur v. High Court of Haryana Through Registrar
cases.principle: Relied on as part of the judicial pronouncements to conclude that prosecution for making false statements should only be invoked when it is expedient in the interest of justice and in exceptional circumstances.

cases.case_name: Chajoo Ram v. Radhey Shyam & Anr.
cases.principle: To expound on when prosecution for giving false evidence should be sanctioned by Courts.

cases.case_name: R.S. Sujatha v. State of Karnataka
cases.principle: Cited for its approval and reliance on previous judgments to establish the law on when prosecution for false statements is justified.

cases.case_name: Bhima Razu Prasad v. State Rep. by Deputy Supdt. of Police, CBI/SPE/ACU-II
cases.principle: Relied on as part of the judicial pronouncements to conclude that prosecution for making false statements should only be invoked when it is expedient in the interest of justice and in exceptional circumstances.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a statement to constitute the offense of giving false evidence, it must be made before an authority that has been expressly deemed to be a ‘Court’.
obiter: A statement, for the purposes of giving false evidence, can be made verbally or otherwise.
A false statement regarding a person's belief is included within the meaning of giving false evidence, just as a false statement about what a person knows.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The statements made in the affidavit do not make it expedient in the interest of justice to initiate prosecution, nor do they constitute the exceptional circumstances required to invoke the powers under the relevant sections, as it cannot be unequivocally held that there was a deliberate falsehood on a matter of substance.
legal_tests_applied: The Court should be of the prima facie opinion that there exists sufficient and reasonable ground to initiate proceedings against the person who has allegedly made a false statement(s);

Such proceedings should be initiated when doing the same is “expedient in the interests of justice to punish the delinquent” and not merely because of inaccuracy in statements that may be innocent/immaterial;
There should be “deliberate falsehood on a matter of substance”;
The Court should be satisfied that there is a reasonable foundation for the charge, with distinct evidence and not mere suspicion;
Proceedings should be initiated in exceptional circumstances, for instance, when a party has perjured themselves to beneficial orders from the Court.
why_respondent_won: The statements in the affidavit do not make it expedient in the interest of justice to prosecute.
The circumstances do not constitute the exceptional circumstances in which such Sections may be invoked.
It cannot be unequivocally held that there was deliberate falsehood on a matter of substance.
policy_considerations: The court should not set the machinery of criminal law in motion unless there are sufficient and reasonable grounds, otherwise, the prosecution degenerates itself into persecution which often is fraught with evil consequences.
